Introduction - February 2010 

##### **Introduction** 

- **_The precious metals sector sustained a price correction in the second half of January, driven by economic considerations and a fresh flight of investors from risk._** 

- **_The PGMs have remained the more resilient metals within the sector by virtue of the initiation of the new exchange traded funds as well as their exposure to the recovering automotive sector._** 

- **_Gold and silver continue to have a better medium-term prognosis as inflationary pressures are still on the horizon and, although the dollar is enjoying a period of s

hort term strength against the euro, it is expected to suffer another downturn later in the year._** - **_Silver is likely to sustain the strongest net performance from early February through to the end of the year but this is in part because it has recently shown its capricious nature with a very sharp fall in price under heavy speculative liquidation._** - **_Silver’s fall came as part of the shudder that went through the commodities sector. Both gold and silver now need some time to consolidate. The recent vulnerability at high prices is undermining sentiment and there is a distinct possibility of another downturn before a sustainable recovery._** - **_Any such weakness in gold and silver is likely to pull platinum and palladium down again (and they are in need of a rest after the ETF-led move) before they, too, recover. Industrial metals were particularly hard hit. Silver’s sharp fall reflects its notoriously volatile nature, as well as the fact that, in the short term at least (and depending on the moods of the markets), silver can swing between being perceived as an industrial metal on one day and a precious metal on another. On average, over the past ten years, jewellery, silverware and coins have together accounted for 34% of global silver demand, with industrial and photographic uses accounting for the balance. The markets are regaining some confidence at the start of February as the knee-jerk reactions of mid-January, exacerbated latterly by technically-driven reading, and has given way to more measured views. The waves of selling in the markets were triggered essentially by two specific features that stirred up underlying unease. The first relates to China and the markets’ realisation that the country is tightening monetary policy. The government has been operating in two ways in the domestic money market in order to try and reduce the amount of bank lending in the system. This is in an effort to prevent the economy, which has been responding to the massive economic stimulus programme (which started in late 2008), from veering toward an inflationary spiral and the development of associated asset bubbles - the property market is already extremely strong and inward investment has been soaring. The reserve ratio increase (by half a point to 16%) was announced in the second week of January and unsettled the equity markets in particular as concerns were raised about the ability of the Chinese economy and what the international ramifications would be if the world’s third largest economy (soon to overtake Japan to become the second largest) started to overheat and then stumble. These concerns were exacerbated when Chinese Stateowned banks were told late in January to suspend lending for a period. The Chinese economy expanded at an annualised 10.7% in the fourth quarter of last year giving full-year growth of 8.7%, well ahead of the target of 8%. At the Davos Economic Forum at the end of January, Chinese Vice Premier Li stated that “despite the fact that local prices are rising once more, the government will continue to maintain a relatively easy monetary policy”, implying that it will continue to try and keep the economy bowling along. The implication is that the government is unlikely to impose draconian tightening measures, but will aim to keep a light hand on the tiller. The second announcement to send alarm bells ringing around the markets in mid-January, was President Obama’s proposals for tighter regulations of the banking sector, especially over proprietary trading. This raised immediate fears that it might have a knock-on effect into the lending market and thus help to stifle a nascent recovery in the United States. The view that now seems to be prevailing is that governments, having come so far in terms of fiscal stimulus in order to stave off a financial melt-down, are unlikely to choke off an early recovery. There was also plenty of selling in evidence as well during the first half of the month, coming from a variety of investment and speculative sources augmented by reports of bouts of arbitrage selling from Shanghai. As a result, gold’s bounce was not entirely convincing and the spot price reached a high January fix of $1,138.25 on the afternoon of 14th January. After a brief period of attempted consolidation above $1,130, gold succumbed to the malaise that spread across a number of asset classes in the second half of January as the markets reacted to a number of developments, notably to President Obama’s banking proposals and increasing evidence of a tightening in Chinese monetary policy. Gold had fallen towards $1,070 by the end of the month before starting to recover and at the start of February the price had regained $1,100. These price ranges are narrow when compared with gold’s strong upward leg in the second half of 2009 and this steepened uptrend channel has not been broken, although it has come perilously close to it. external indicators are mixed. Physical demand has picked up in important regional consuming areas, notably India and China, but the market is aware that the Chinese New Year is imminent and there is therefore an element of concern that this recent boost in demand may prove to be short-lived. With the euro under pressure, as investors take a dim view of the relative outlook for the European economy and uncertainties persist over the situation in Greece and how it will be handled, there is a renewed, if underlying, aversion to risk. This is staying the hands of professional gold speculators as the dollar is thus expected to continue to remain strong in the near term, although here, too, there are elements of uncertainty as President Obama presents his Budget proposals to Congress. Gold tends to thrive on market uncertainty and therefore in early February there are well founded arguments both for renewed strength in the price for the medium term and also for a rather more anaemic short-term outlook. Investment demand, by contrast, has picked up smartly and imports have also strengthened. GFMS estimates, as detailed in January’s _Gold Survey 2009 - Update 2_ , that China became the world’s largest gold bar hoarder in 2009; early indications in 2010 suggest that gold bar hoarding demand has remained strong early in the year. **Ag4** Independent - Informed - International Platinum and Palladium - February 2010 ##### **Platinum and Palladium** ###### **Introduction** Attention in the platinum and palladium markets has been dominated recently by the launch of the new exchange traded funds in New York (ticker symbols PPLT and PALL) on 8th January. The anticipation of these funds was largely responsible for the outperformance of platinum and palladium against gold and silver during December and the uptake of metal into the funds over January sustained this strong performance as the flows of funds were substantial, to say the least. Sentiment was further bolstered by a number of automobile production figures, which (with the possible exception of Europe) have generally been surprising to the upside and boosting the markets’ expect

ation for demand, while industrial re-stocking has also been a supportive factor. 

There is a distinct probability that these metals prices will correct as this investment momentum wanes as there has already been a noticeable price-elastic response in the jewellery sector that has increased the onus on investment to keep prices high.  Indeed as we write the ETF momentum already appears to be slowing.  It is also worth noting that while the New York palladium fund has exploded on to the scene, the palladium funds in Europe have suffered some attrition and so the net increase, while still impressive, is not quite as much as the New York figures, taken in isolation, would suggest.  This is considered in more detail in the following pages. 

Platinum is expected to generate a surplus of mine+scrap supply over industrial fabrication demand this year, and while palladium is likely to be in a gross deficit on the same basis, it is likely that more shipments out of Russian State inventories will mean that the residual market will be in 

surplus – although a degree of restocking in the consuming industries, notably the auto sector, will help to reduce this when considered in terms of industrial purchases.  The rate of uptake into the PGM ETFs on aggregate during January was clearly very strong and has absorbed a good proportion of these projected surpluses, but it would be unwise to assume that these funds will always be able to mop up any excess that the markets might generate, especially if high prices not only constrain jewellery demand but generate increased scrap return. 

###### **Price action; spikes possible in both metals, but falls to follow** 

After correcting in December, but to a lesser extent than gold and silver, platinum prices started January on a strong note and continued to rise until the 19th of the month when it was caught in the storm that blew through a number of asset classes as investors took fright once more and risk-aversion came to the fore.  The opening fix of the year was $1,496.00 and on 19th January platinum reached an intra-day high of $1,650, a gain of 10% over the period and some 116% higher than the low of $763 registered in late October 2008. Trading was relatively thin in the first half of the month, suggesting that perhaps the market participants were uncertain as to whether platinum could sustain these higher prices.  It is particularly interesting to note that in the week to the 12th January, before the price actually topped out, the there was a large jump in the outright short positions held by “large-scale” non-commercial traders on NYMEX. The fact that the price went on rising (and that there had been no corresponding increase in shorts among either trade participants or smaller-scale speculative interests) suggests that a market player or players may have been taking a view about the impact on the price of the listing of the new ETF, and looking to benefit from any subsequent recoil in price.
